chapters.title: The Gathering
paragraphs: As for what you're asking about, I believe I'm well prepared to answer. In fact, the day before yesterday I was on my way into the city from my home in Phalerum when an acquaintance of mine caught sight of me from behind and called out playfully from a distance, 'Apollodorus! You there — you Phalerian! Halt!' So I did as I was told, and he said, 'Apollodorus, I was just looking for you. I wanted to ask you about the speeches in praise of love that Socrates, Alcibiades, and others gave at Agathon's supper. Someone told me what he had heard from Phoenix, the son of Philip, but his account was very vague. He did say, though, that you knew about them, so I'd like to hear them from you. Who better than you to report your friend's words? But first tell me,' he said, 'were you at that gathering yourself?'
'Glaucon,' I said, 'your informant must have been very vague indeed, if you imagine that the occasion was recent, or that I could have been one of the party.'
'Well, yes,' he replied, 'I did think so.'

'Impossible,' I said. 'Don't you know that Agathon hasn't lived in Athens for many years, and that it's not yet three years since I started spending time with Socrates and made it my daily business to know everything he says and does? There was a time when I ran around from one thing to another, thinking I was doing something worthwhile, but I was really a thoroughly wretched creature — no better than you are now. I thought I ought to do anything rather than be a philosopher.'
'Well,' he said, 'joking aside, tell me when that gathering took place.'
'When we were still boys,' I replied, 'at the time Agathon won the prize with his first tragedy. It was the day after he and his chorus had offered their victory sacrifice.'
'Then it must have been a long time ago,' he said. 'And who told you — was it Socrates?'

'No, not Socrates,' I replied. 'It was the same man who told Phoenix — Aristodemus, of the deme of Cydathenaeum, a little fellow who never wore shoes. He had been at Agathon's feast, and I think that in those days no one was a more devoted admirer of Socrates. What's more, I have asked Socrates himself whether some parts of Aristodemus's account were true, and he confirmed them.' 'Then,' said Glaucon, 'let's hear the story. Isn't the road to Athens just made for conversation?' So we walked along and talked about the speeches on love. And that is why, as I told you at the start, I'm well prepared to do what you ask; I'll go through them again for you, if you like. For speaking about philosophy, or hearing others speak about it, always gives me the greatest pleasure — to say nothing of the benefit. But when I hear any other kind of talk — especially the talk of rich men and businessmen like you — it annoys me; and I pity you, my friends, because you think you're doing something when in reality you're doing nothing. I suppose you pity me in return and think I'm miserable — and very probably you're right. But what you only think about me, I know for certain about you. That's the difference.

COMPANION: I see you're just the same as ever, Apollodorus — always speaking ill of yourself and of others. I really do believe you pity all mankind except Socrates, starting with yourself. In this you live up to your old nickname, 'Apollodorus the madman.' I don't know how you came by it, but it suits you, for you're always raging against yourself and everybody except Socrates.
APOLLODORUS: Yes, friend, and the reason people say I'm crazy and out of my mind is precisely that I hold these views about you and about myself. No other evidence is needed.
COMPANION: Enough of that, Apollodorus. Let me renew my request and ask you to repeat the conversation for me.
APOLLODORUS: Well, the tale of love went like this — but perhaps I should start from the beginning and try to give you the exact words of Aristodemus.
He said that he met Socrates fresh from the bath and wearing sandals — an unusual sight — so he asked him where he was going, looking so fine.

'To a banquet at Agathon's,' he replied. 'I turned down his invitation yesterday — his victory sacrifice — because I was afraid of a crowd, but I promised to come today instead. So I've put on my finery, because he's such a fine man. What do you say — will you come along unasked?'
'I'll do whatever you tell me,' Aristodemus replied.
'Follow me, then,' said Socrates, 'and let's demolish the proverb:
'"To the feasts of inferior men the good unbidden go;"
'and instead — since Agathon's name means "good" — our version will run:
'"To the feasts of the good the good unbidden go;"

'and we can support this change by the authority of Homer himself, who not only demolishes the proverb but positively outrages it. He portrays Agamemnon as the bravest of warriors and Menelaus as a fainthearted one; yet when Agamemnon is offering sacrifice and giving a feast, he has Menelaus come uninvited to Agamemnon's banquet — the worse man to the feast of the better, not the better to the worse.'
'I'm rather afraid, Socrates,' said Aristodemus, 'that this may be my case after all — that, like Menelaus in Homer, I shall be the inferior person who
'"To the feasts of the wise unbidden goes."
'But I'll say that you invited me, and then you'll have to make the excuse for me.'
'Two going together,'
he replied, in Homeric style, 'one or the other of them can think up an excuse on the way.'

This was the kind of conversation they had as they went along. Then Socrates, lost in thought, dropped behind, and told Aristodemus, who was waiting for him, to go on ahead. When Aristodemus reached Agathon's house, he found the doors wide open, and a comical thing happened. A servant coming out met him and led him at once into the dining room, where the guests were already reclining, for the dinner was about to begin. 'Welcome, Aristodemus,' said Agathon as soon as he appeared. 'You are just in time to dine with us. If you've come about anything else, put it off and join us — I was looking for you yesterday to invite you, but I couldn't find you. But what have you done with Socrates?'
Aristodemus turned around, but Socrates was nowhere to be seen. So he had to explain that Socrates had been with him only a moment before, and that it was Socrates who had invited him to the dinner.
'You were quite right in coming,' said Agathon, 'but where is he himself?'
'He was right behind me just now, as I came in,' said Aristodemus, 'and I can't think what has become of him.'
'Go and look for him, boy,' said Agathon, 'and bring him in. And you, Aristodemus, take the place by Eryximachus in the meantime.'

The servant then helped him wash, and he lay down. Soon another servant came in and reported that our friend Socrates had withdrawn into the porch of the house next door. 'He's standing there, stock-still,' the servant said, 'and when I call to him he won't come.'
'How strange,' said Agathon. 'Then you must call him again, and keep calling him.'

'Leave him alone,' said Aristodemus, my informant. 'He has a habit of stopping wherever he happens to be and standing there, lost in thought, for no reason. I believe he will soon appear, so don't disturb him.'

'Well, if you think so, I'll leave him alone,' said Agathon. And then, turning to the servants, he added, 'Serve dinner without waiting for him. Serve whatever you like, since there's no one to give you orders; I have never left you to yourselves before, but on this occasion imagine that you are the hosts, and that I and the company are your guests. Treat us well, and we'll praise you.' After this, dinner was served, but still no Socrates. During the meal Agathon several times wanted to send for him, but Aristodemus wouldn't let him. At last, when the dinner was about half over — for, as usual, his spell of thought did not last long — Socrates came in. Agathon, who was reclining alone at the end of the table, begged him to take the place next to him. 'So that I can touch you,' he said, 'and get the benefit of the wise thought that came to you in the porch; for I am certain that you would not have come away until you had found what you were looking for, and that you have it now.'

'How I wish,' said Socrates, taking the place he was offered, 'that wisdom could flow by touch from the fuller of us into the emptier, the way water flows along a thread of wool from a fuller cup into an emptier one. If that were so, how highly I would value the privilege of reclining beside you! For you would fill me with a stream of rich and beautiful wisdom. My own wisdom is a poor and doubtful sort of thing, no better than a dream; but yours is brilliant and full of promise — it shone out in all the splendor of youth the day before yesterday, in front of more than thirty thousand Greeks.'
'You are mocking me, Socrates,' said Agathon. 'Before long you and I will have to settle which of us is wiser, and Dionysus shall be the judge. But for now, you'd better attend to your dinner.'

Socrates took his place on the couch and dined with the rest. Then libations of wine were poured, a hymn was sung to the god, and the other customary rites were performed; and they were about to start drinking when Pausanias said, 'Now, my friends, how can we drink with the least harm to ourselves? I can tell you that I am still suffering badly from yesterday's drinking, and need time to recover; and I suspect most of you are in the same state, since you were at the party yesterday. So consider: how can we make the drinking as easy as possible?'
'I entirely agree,' said Aristophanes, 'that we should by all means avoid hard drinking, for I was myself one of those who were yesterday drowned in drink.'
'I think that you are right,' said Eryximachus, the son of Acumenus. 'But I should still like to hear one other person speak: is Agathon able to drink hard?'
'I am not equal to it,' said Agathon.

'Then,' said Eryximachus, 'those of us with weak heads — myself, Aristodemus, Phaedrus and the others who never can drink much — are lucky that the stronger drinkers are not in a drinking mood. I don't count Socrates: he can either drink or not, and won't mind whichever we do. Well, since none of the company seems inclined to drink much, perhaps you will forgive me if I tell you, as a physician, that heavy drinking is a bad habit. I never drink deeply myself if I can help it, and I certainly wouldn't recommend it to anyone else — least of all to someone still suffering from yesterday's party.'
'I always do what you advise,' said Phaedrus, of the deme of Myrrhinus, 'especially when you advise as a physician; and the rest of the company will do the same, if they are wise.'
It was agreed that drinking was not to be the order of the day, but that they were all to drink only so much as they pleased.

'Then,' said Eryximachus, 'since you are all agreed that everyone should drink as much as he likes, and that nobody is to be forced, I propose next that we send away the flute-girl who has just come in: let her play to herself, or, if she prefers, to the women in the house. Today let us spend our time in conversation instead; and, if you will allow me, I will tell you what sort of conversation I have in mind.' Everyone agreed, and Eryximachus went on:
'I will begin,' he said, 'as Melanippe does in Euripides:
'"Not mine the word" —

'which I am about to speak, but that of Phaedrus. For he often says to me indignantly, "Isn't it strange, Eryximachus, that the other gods have poems and hymns composed in their honor, while the great and glorious god Love has not had a single poet, among all our many poets, to sing his praises? And there are the worthy sophists, too — the excellent Prodicus, for example — who have written prose speeches in praise of Heracles and other heroes; and, what is still more extraordinary, I once came across a philosophical book in which the usefulness of salt was made the subject of an eloquent speech, and many other such things have been honored in the same way. To think that people should have taken such trouble over these things, and yet that to this day no one has ever dared to sing Love's praises as he deserves! So completely has this great god been neglected." Now I think Phaedrus is quite right about this, and so I want to offer him a contribution; and I also think that we who are gathered here could do nothing better at this moment than honor the god Love. If you agree, we shall have plenty to talk about. I propose that each of us in turn, going from left to right, should make a speech in honor of Love, the best he can; and Phaedrus should begin, because he is sitting first on the left and because he is the father of the idea.'

'No one will vote against you, Eryximachus,' said Socrates. 'How could I oppose your motion, when I claim to understand nothing but matters of love? Nor, I presume, will Agathon and Pausanias; and certainly not Aristophanes, whose whole life is taken up with Dionysus and Aphrodite; nor anyone else I see here. The arrangement, I know, may seem rather hard on those of us whose places are last; but we shall be satisfied if the speakers before us make good speeches. Let Phaedrus begin the praise of Love, and good luck to him.' All the others agreed, and told Phaedrus to do as Socrates said.
Aristodemus did not recollect all that was said, nor do I recollect all that he related to me; but I will tell you what I thought most worthy of remembrance, and what the chief speakers said.

chapters.title: Phaedrus's Speech
paragraphs: Phaedrus began by declaring that Love is a mighty god, a wonder among gods and men, and most wonderful of all in his birth. For he is the oldest of the gods, and that is an honor to him. One proof of his claim to this honor is that there is no record of his parents: no poet or prose writer has ever said that he had any. As Hesiod says:
'First Chaos came, and then broad-bosomed Earth, the everlasting seat of all that is, and Love.'
In other words, after Chaos came these two, Earth and Love. And Parmenides sings of Generation, the power that brings things to birth:
'First in the train of gods, he fashioned Love.'

Acusilaus agrees with Hesiod. So there are many witnesses who acknowledge that Love is the oldest of the gods. And he is not only the oldest; he is also the source of our greatest blessings. For I know of no greater blessing for a young man starting out in life than a virtuous lover, and none greater for a lover than a beloved youth. There is a principle that ought to guide anyone who means to live nobly, and nothing can instill it so well as love — not family ties, not public honors, not wealth, nor anything else. What principle do I mean? A sense of honor and of shame, without which no city and no individual ever does any great or good work. I say that if a lover were caught doing something dishonorable, or submitting through cowardice to dishonor at someone else's hands, he would be more pained at being seen by his beloved than by his father, his companions, or anyone else. And the beloved, too, when he is caught in some disgraceful situation, feels the same way about his lover. If only there were some way of forming a city or an army of lovers and their beloveds! They would govern their own city better than anyone, avoiding everything dishonorable and competing with one another for honor; and fighting side by side, even a mere handful of them would conquer the world.

For what lover would not rather be seen by all mankind than by his beloved when deserting his post or throwing away his weapons? He would die a thousand deaths sooner than endure that. And who would abandon his beloved, or fail him in the hour of danger? At such a moment even the worst coward would become an inspired hero, as brave as the bravest: Love would inspire him. The courage that, as Homer says, the god breathes into the souls of some heroes, Love by his very nature instills in the lover.

Love will make men dare to die for the one they love — only love will — and women as well as men. Alcestis, the daughter of Pelias, stands before all Greece as proof of this. She was willing to die for her husband when no one else would, though he had a father and a mother; and her love so far exceeded theirs in tenderness that she made them seem like strangers to their own son, related to him in name only. What she did seemed so noble, to the gods as well as to men, that the gods, in admiration, granted her a privilege they have given to very few of the many who have acted nobly: they allowed her to return alive to earth. So greatly do the gods honor devotion and virtue in love. But Orpheus, the harper, the son of Oeagrus, they sent away empty-handed. They showed him only a phantom of the woman he had come for, and would not give him the woman herself, because he showed no courage. He was only a harp-player; he did not dare, like Alcestis, to die for love, but schemed to enter Hades alive. And later, as punishment for his cowardice, they had him put to death at the hands of women.

Very different was the reward the gods gave to the true love of Achilles for Patroclus. Patroclus was the lover, and Achilles the beloved. (Aeschylus makes a foolish mistake when he says that Patroclus was the beloved: Achilles was surely the more beautiful of the two — more beautiful than all the other heroes, too — and, as Homer tells us, he was still beardless and much younger.) Greatly as the gods honor virtue in love, they admire, value and reward it even more when the beloved returns the lover's love; for the lover is more divine, because he is inspired by a god. Now Achilles knew, because his mother had told him, that if he held back from killing Hector he could escape death, go home and live to a ripe old age. Nevertheless he gave his life to avenge his friend: he dared to die not only for him but after him, when Patroclus was already dead. That is why the gods honored him even above Alcestis, and sent him to the Islands of the Blessed. These are my reasons for declaring that Love is the oldest, the noblest and the mightiest of the gods, and the chief source and giver of virtue in life and of happiness after death.

chapters.title: Pausanias's Speech
paragraphs: This, or something close to it, was Phaedrus's speech. Several other speeches followed that Aristodemus couldn't remember, but the next one he recounted was Pausanias's. Pausanias began: Phaedrus, I don't think the question has been framed quite correctly. We shouldn't be asked to praise Love in such an undiscriminating way. If there were only one Love, what you said would be fine — but since there are more Loves than one, we should have started by deciding which of them we are praising. Let me fix this oversight. First I'll tell you which Love deserves our praise, and then I'll try to hymn that praiseworthy one in a manner worthy of him. For we all know that Love is inseparable from Aphrodite, and if there were only one Aphrodite there would be only one Love — but since there are two goddesses, there must be two Loves. And am I not right that there are two goddesses? The elder, who has no mother, is called the Heavenly Aphrodite — she is the daughter of Uranus. The younger, the daughter of Zeus and Dione, we call Common; and the Love who works alongside her is rightly named Common, just as the other love is called Heavenly. All the gods deserve praise, but not without distinguishing their natures — so I must try to distinguish the characters of the two Loves. Now, actions vary in value according to how they are performed.

Take, for example, what we are doing right now — drinking, singing, and talking. These actions are not in themselves either good or evil; they turn out one way or the other depending on how they are done. Done well, they are good; done badly, they are evil. In the same way, not every love is noble and worthy of praise — only the love that has a noble purpose. The Love who is the offspring of the Common Aphrodite is essentially common and makes no distinctions. This is the love the baser sort of men feel; it tends to be directed at women as well as at youths, and it is of the body rather than the soul. The most foolish beings are the objects of this love, which cares only about getting what it wants and never about achieving its end nobly, and so it does good and evil quite indiscriminately. The goddess who is this Love's mother is far younger than the other, and she was born of the union of male and female, sharing in both. But the offspring of the Heavenly Aphrodite comes from a mother in whose birth the female had no part — she is from the male only. This is the love that is directed toward youths, and because the goddess is older, there is nothing of wantonness in her. Those inspired by this love turn to the male, delighting in whoever has the more valiant and intelligent nature; and anyone can recognize those who are truly inspired by it from the very character of their attachments.

For they love not boys, but intelligent beings whose reason is beginning to develop — around the age when their beards begin to grow. And in choosing young men as their companions, they mean to be faithful to them, to spend their whole lives with them — not to catch them in their inexperience, deceive them, make fools of them, or run from one to another. The love of young boys, however, ought to be forbidden by law, because their future is uncertain: they may turn out good or bad, in body or soul, and much noble enthusiasm may be wasted on them. In this matter the good are a law to themselves, but the coarser sort of lovers ought to be restrained by force — just as we try to restrain them from fixing their affections on freeborn women. These are the people who bring reproach upon love; and some have been led to deny the lawfulness of such attachments because they see the impropriety and evil in them; for surely nothing done decorously and lawfully can justly be censured.

Now here in Athens, and in Sparta, the rules about love are perplexing, but in most cities they are simple and easy to grasp. In Elis and Boeotia, and in countries that have no gift for eloquence, the rules are very straightforward — the law is simply in favor of these connections, and no one, young or old, says a word against them. The reason, I suppose, is that the men there are not eloquent, so lovers prefer not to take the trouble of pleading their case. In Ionia, on the other hand, and in other places generally subject to the barbarians, the custom is held to be dishonorable. There, the love of youths shares the evil reputation attached to philosophy and physical training, because all three are hostile to tyranny. Rulers' interests require that their subjects be poor in spirit and that no strong bond of friendship or fellowship form among them — and love, more than any other motive, is likely to inspire such bonds, as our own Athenian tyrants learned by experience. For Aristogeiton's love and Harmodius's constancy proved strong enough to bring down their power.

And so the ill repute into which these attachments have fallen in some places must be attributed to the bad character of those who condemn them — that is, to the self-seeking of the rulers and the cowardice of the ruled. On the other hand, the indiscriminate honor given to them in other countries is owing to the mental laziness of those who hold that opinion. In our own country a far better principle prevails, though, as I said, it's a rather perplexing one. Consider: open loves are held to be more honorable than secret ones, and the love of the noblest and highest is especially honorable, even when the beloved is less beautiful than others. Consider too the enormous encouragement the whole world gives the lover: he is not thought to be doing anything dishonorable — if he succeeds he is praised, and if he fails he is blamed. And in pursuing his love, custom allows him to do many strange things that philosophy would bitterly condemn if they were done from any motive of profit, or desire for office, or power.

He may plead, beg, implore, swear oaths, sleep on a mat at the door, and endure a slavery worse than any slave's. In any other situation his friends and enemies alike would step in to stop him; but here no friend will be ashamed of him or admonish him, and no enemy will accuse him of meanness or flattery. The actions of a lover have a grace that ennobles them, and custom has decided they are highly commendable and bring no loss of character. And strangest of all, he alone may swear an oath and break it — so people say — and the gods will forgive his transgression, for there is no such thing as a lover's oath. Such is the complete liberty that gods and men have allowed the lover, according to the custom that prevails in our part of the world. From this point of view a man could fairly argue that in Athens to love and to be loved is considered a most honorable thing. But then again — when parents forbid their sons to speak with their lovers and place them under a tutor whose job is to prevent any such thing, and when their companions and peers taunt them for anything of the sort they observe, and their elders refuse to silence or rebuke those who taunt them — anyone reflecting on all this would, on the contrary, conclude that we hold these practices to be utterly disgraceful.

But as I was saying at the start, the truth, I think, is this: whether such practices are honorable or dishonorable is not a simple question. They are honorable to whoever pursues them honorably, and dishonorable to whoever pursues them dishonorably. There is dishonor in yielding to the bad, or yielding in a bad way; but there is honor in yielding to the good, or yielding in an honorable way. The bad lover is the common lover, who loves the body rather than the soul — he is not even stable, because he loves something that is itself unstable, so when the bloom of youth he desired is gone, he takes wing and flies away, breaking all his words and promises. But the love of a noble disposition lasts a lifetime, for it becomes one with what is everlasting. The custom of our country would have both kinds of lover thoroughly tested, and would have us yield to the one sort and avoid the other; and therefore it encourages some to pursue and others to flee, testing both the lover and the beloved in contests and trials until it becomes clear which class each of them belongs to.

This is why, in the first place, a hasty attachment is considered dishonorable: time is the true test, here as in most other things. And secondly, there is dishonor in being overcome by the love of money, wealth, or political power — whether a man is frightened into surrender by losing them, or, having tasted the benefits of money and political corruption, cannot rise above their seductions. For none of these things is permanent or lasting, and besides, no noble friendship ever sprang from them. There remains, then, only one honorable way, allowed by custom, for the beloved to yield — the way of virtue. For just as we granted that any service the lover renders to his beloved is not to be counted as flattery or as a dishonor to himself, so the beloved has one, and only one, form of voluntary service that is not dishonorable: namely, virtuous service.

For we have a custom according to which, if someone serves another in the belief that he will be improved by him — whether in wisdom or in some other aspect of virtue — such voluntary service is not to be considered a dishonor, and it is not open to the charge of flattery. These two customs — the love of youths, and the practice of philosophy and virtue generally — ought to meet in one; and when they do, the beloved may honorably yield to the lover. For when lover and beloved come together, each following his own law: the lover thinking he is right to do any service he can for the beloved who yields to him, and the beloved thinking he is right to show any kindness he can to the one who is making him wise and good — the first capable of communicating wisdom and virtue, the second seeking to acquire them for the sake of his education and wisdom — then, when the two laws of love are fulfilled and meet in one, and only then, may the beloved yield honorably to the lover. And when love is of this unselfish sort, there is no disgrace in being deceived; but in every other case there is equal disgrace in being deceived or not. For if someone yields to a lover under the impression that he is rich, and then gets nothing because the lover turns out to be poor, he is disgraced just the same — because he has done his best to show that he would give himself up to anyone's 'uses base' — would let anyone use him basely — for the sake of money; and that is not honorable.

By the same principle, a man who gives himself to a lover because he believes him to be a good man, hoping to be improved by his company, shows himself to be virtuous even if the object of his affection turns out to be a scoundrel with no virtue at all. If he is deceived, his error is a noble one. For he has proved that on his side he will do anything for anyone with a view to virtue and self-improvement — and nothing can be nobler than that. Noble, then, in every case, is the acceptance of another for the sake of virtue. This is the love of the Heavenly Goddess — heavenly love, of great worth to individuals and to cities, making lover and beloved alike earnest in the work of their own improvement. All other loves are the offspring of the other goddess, the Common one. To you, Phaedrus, I offer this contribution of mine in praise of Love, the best I could make on short notice.

Pausanias paused — a play on words of the balanced kind the wise have taught me to use. Aristodemus said that Aristophanes was supposed to speak next, but either from eating too much or for some other reason he had the hiccups and had to switch turns with Eryximachus the physician, who was reclining on the couch just below him. 'Eryximachus,' Aristophanes said, 'you ought either to cure my hiccups or speak in my turn until they stop.'

'I'll do both,' said Eryximachus. 'I'll speak in your turn, and you can speak in mine; and while I'm speaking, I recommend that you hold your breath. If after a while the hiccups haven't gotten better, then gargle a little water; and if they still persist, tickle your nose with something and sneeze — once or twice should do it, and even the most violent hiccups are sure to stop.' 'I'll do as you prescribe,' said Aristophanes. 'Now get on with it.'

chapters.title: Eryximachus's Speech
paragraphs: Eryximachus spoke as follows: Since Pausanias made a fine beginning but a lame ending, I must try to make up for what he left out. I think he was right to distinguish two kinds of love. But my own art tells me more: this double love is not only a feeling in human souls, directed toward beautiful people or toward other things; it is found in the bodies of all animals and in everything that grows from the earth — in everything that exists, I might say. That is the conclusion I seem to have reached from my own art of medicine, which teaches me how great and wonderful and universal the god of love is, and how his rule extends over all things, divine as well as human. I will begin with medicine, to do honor to my art. The human body contains these two kinds of love. They are admittedly different and unlike, and being unlike, they love and desire unlike things: what is healthy in the body desires one thing, and what is diseased desires another. Pausanias was saying just now that it is honorable to gratify good men and dishonorable to gratify bad ones. So too in the body, the good and healthy elements should be gratified, while the bad and diseased elements should not be gratified, but discouraged.

This is what the physician has to do, and it is what the art of medicine consists in. For medicine may be described, in general, as knowledge of the body's loves and desires, and of how to satisfy them or not. The best physician is the one who can tell the noble love from the base, or can turn one into the other; and whoever knows how to remove love and how to implant it, as needed, and can reconcile the most hostile elements in the body and make them love each other, is a skilled practitioner. The most hostile elements are the most opposite: hot and cold, bitter and sweet, wet and dry, and the like. My ancestor Asclepius knew how to create friendship and harmony among these, and so he founded our art, as our friends the poets here tell us — and I believe them. Not only medicine in all its branches, but physical training and farming as well, are under the rule of love. Anyone who gives the matter the slightest attention will also see that in music there is the same reconciliation of opposites. I suppose that must be what Heraclitus meant, though he did not put it accurately. He says that the One is held together by being at odds with itself, like the harmony of the bow and of the lyre, whose parts pull against each other. But it is absurd to say that harmony is discord, or that it is made of elements that are still in discord.

But what he probably meant was that harmony is made of high and low notes that once disagreed but have now been reconciled by the art of music. If the high and low notes still disagreed, there could be no harmony — clearly not. For harmony is consonance, and consonance is an agreement; and there cannot be agreement between things that disagree while they still disagree. What is still in discord cannot be harmonized. In the same way, rhythm is made of short and long elements that once differed and now agree. In all these cases it is music that creates this agreement, as medicine does in the body: it makes love and concord grow among them. So music, too, is concerned with the principles of love as they apply to harmony and rhythm. In the basic structure of harmony and rhythm, it is easy to see love at work, and here love has not yet become double. But when you have to put them to use in real life — whether in composing songs, or in the correct performance of melodies and meters already composed, the latter of which is called education — then the difficulty begins, and a good practitioner is needed.

Then the old story has to be told again. There is the noble, heavenly love, the love that belongs to Urania, the beautiful and heavenly Muse: we must favor the self-controlled, and favor those who are not yet self-controlled only so that they may become so, and we must preserve their love. And there is the common love, which belongs to the Muse Polyhymnia: it must be handled with caution, so that its pleasure can be enjoyed without breeding licentiousness, just as in my own art it is an important matter to regulate a gourmet's appetites so that he can enjoy his food without the illness that would otherwise follow. So I conclude that in music, in medicine, and in all other things, human and divine, we must keep watch on both loves as far as we can, for both are present.

The seasons of the year, too, are full of both these loves. When the elements I mentioned — hot and cold, wet and dry — come to love one another in harmony and blend with moderation, they bring health and plenty to people, animals and plants, and do them no harm. But when the unruly love gets the upper hand and takes hold of the seasons, it does great damage and harm. It is the source of plagues and brings many other kinds of disease on animals and plants; for frost and hail and blight all spring from the excess and disorder of these loves among the elements. Knowledge of these loves as they relate to the movements of the heavenly bodies and the seasons of the year is called astronomy. Furthermore, all sacrifices and everything that belongs to divination — the art by which gods and men communicate — are concerned only with preserving the good love and curing the bad. For every kind of impiety is likely to follow if a man does not favor, honor and revere the harmonious love in all he does, but honors the other love instead, whether in his feelings toward gods or parents, the living or the dead. So the task of divination is to watch over these loves and heal them; and divination is the peacemaker between gods and men, because it knows which human loves lead toward piety and which toward impiety. So great and mighty — or rather, all-powerful — is the force of love as a whole.

But above all, the love that is concerned with the good, and is perfected together with self-control and justice, among gods or among men, has the greatest power. It is the source of all our happiness and harmony, and makes us friends with the gods above us and with one another. I dare say that I too have left out a good deal that might be said in praise of Love, but not intentionally. Now, Aristophanes, it is up to you to fill the gaps, or else to praise the god in some other way — for I see that your hiccups are gone.

'Yes,' said Aristophanes, who spoke next, 'my hiccups are gone — but not until I tried sneezing. It makes me wonder whether the body's harmony has a love of noises and ticklings like that, because as soon as I sneezed I was cured.'

Eryximachus said: 'Careful, my friend Aristophanes. You are about to speak, and you are making fun of me. So I shall have to watch your speech and see whether I can find something to laugh at, when you might have spoken in peace.'

'You're right,' said Aristophanes, laughing. 'I take back what I said. But please don't watch me. What I'm afraid of in the speech I'm about to give is not that people will laugh with me — that would be all to the good, and natural to my comic Muse — but that they will only laugh at me.'

'Do you think you can take your shot and get away with it, Aristophanes?' said Eryximachus. 'Well, perhaps if you are very careful, and remember that you will have to answer for what you say, I may be persuaded to let you off.'

chapters.title: Aristophanes's Speech
paragraphs: Aristophanes said that he meant to take a different line, and to praise Love in a way unlike that of either Pausanias or Eryximachus. He began: Human beings, I think, have never understood the power of Love at all, judging by how they neglect him. If they had understood him, they would surely have built him magnificent temples and altars, and offered him solemn sacrifices; but none of this is done, though it certainly ought to be, since of all the gods he is the best friend of human beings, their helper, and the healer of the ills that stand most in the way of human happiness. I will try to explain his power to you, and you shall teach the rest of the world what I teach you. First I must tell you about human nature and what has happened to it; for the original human nature was not what it is now, but different. To begin with, there were three sexes, not two as there are now: male, female, and a third that was a union of the two. Its name, which describes this double nature, survives, but the kind itself has vanished; and 'androgynous' is now only a term of abuse. Second, these first human beings were round, their backs and sides forming a circle. Each had four hands and as many feet, and one head with two faces, exactly alike, looking in opposite directions on a round neck; it had four ears, two sets of genitals, and everything else to match.

Each could walk upright, as we do now, backward or forward as it pleased; and when it wanted to run fast, it could roll over and over at great speed on its four hands and four feet — eight limbs in all — like acrobats turning cartwheels with their legs in the air. There were three sexes, and they were as I have described, because the sun, the moon and the earth are three. The male was originally the child of the sun, the female the child of the earth, and the one that was both male and female was the child of the moon, which is made up of sun and earth. They were round, and they moved round and round, like their parents. Their strength and power were terrible, and their pride was enormous, and they made an attack on the gods. It is of them that the story of Otys and Ephialtes is told — the two who, as Homer says, dared to climb up to heaven and would have laid hands on the gods. The gods held council and did not know what to do. If they killed them and wiped out the race with thunderbolts, as they had the Giants, there would be an end of the sacrifices and worship that human beings offered them; but they could not let this insolence go unchecked either. At last, after a good deal of thought, Zeus found a way. He said: 'I think I have a plan that will humble their pride and improve their manners. They shall go on living, but I will cut each of them in two. That will make them weaker, and at the same time more numerous, which will have the advantage of making them more profitable to us.

'They shall walk upright on two legs; and if they go on being insolent and will not keep quiet, I will split them again, and they shall hop about on one leg.' With that he cut them in two, like a sorb-apple halved for pickling, or an egg sliced with a hair. As he cut each one, he told Apollo to turn its face, with half its neck, around toward the cut side, so that it could look at where it had been cut and learn humility. He also told Apollo to heal their wounds and put their bodies into shape. So Apollo turned the face around, and pulled the skin together from all sides over what we now call the belly, like a drawstring purse, and made a single opening in the middle, which he tied off in a knot — the navel, as it is called. He smoothed out most of the wrinkles and shaped the chest, much as a shoemaker smooths leather on a last; but he left a few wrinkles around the belly and navel, as a reminder of their ancient state. After the division, each half longed for its other half and came back to it; they threw their arms around each other, wound themselves together, and longed to grow into one again, until they were dying of hunger and self-neglect, because they would not do anything apart. And whenever one half died and the other was left, the survivor went looking for another partner — a man or a woman, as we now call them, being halves of whole men or whole women — and clung to it.

They were being destroyed, when Zeus took pity on them and came up with a new plan. He moved their genitals around to the front — they had not always been there — so that they no longer sowed their seed in the ground, as grasshoppers do, but in one another. After this change the male begot offspring in the female, so that when a man and a woman embraced, they would conceive and the race would continue; and when a man came together with a man, they would be satisfied, and rest, and go back to the business of life. That is how long ago the desire for one another was implanted in human beings: it brings us back to our original nature, making one out of two and healing the human condition. Each of us, then, cut off from the other and having only one side, like a flatfish, is only half a human being — one half of a token broken in two, which matches the other half — and each of us is always looking for his other half. Men who are halves of the double kind once called androgynous are lovers of women; most adulterers come from this kind, and so do the adulterous women who lust after men. Women who are halves of the original woman do not care for men but are attached to women; women who take female lovers are of this kind. But those who are halves of the original male pursue males. While they are young, being slices of the original male, they seek out men's company and embrace them; and they are the best of the boys and youths, because they have the most manly nature.

Some people call them shameless, but that is not true. They behave this way not from any lack of shame, but because they are brave and manly and have a manly look, and they embrace what is like themselves. When they grow up, these, and these alone, become our statesmen — which is strong proof of what I am saying. When they reach manhood they are lovers of youths, and by nature they have no interest in marrying and having children; if they do it at all, it is only because the law requires it, and they would be content to live with one another unmarried. A man of this nature is always ready to love and to return love, always embracing what is akin to him. And when one of them meets his other half — his own actual half, whether he is a lover of youths or a lover of another kind — the pair are overwhelmed by an astonishing love, friendship and intimacy, and will not, so to speak, let each other out of sight even for a moment. These are the people who spend their whole lives together, and yet they could not explain what they want from each other. For the intense longing each has for the other does not seem to be the desire for sex, but for something else: the soul of each clearly desires something it cannot put into words, and has only a dim and uncertain sense of what it is.

Suppose Hephaestus came with his tools to the two of them as they lay side by side, and asked, 'What is it you people want from each other?' They would not be able to say. And suppose that, seeing them at a loss, he asked again: 'Do you want to be wholly one — to be together day and night, never apart? If that is what you want, I am ready to melt you into one and let you grow together, so that the two of you become one: as long as you live, you would live a single shared life, as if you were one person, and after you die, down in the underworld, you would still be one soul instead of two. Is this what you long for? Would this satisfy you?' Not one of them, on hearing this offer, would refuse it; each would recognize that this meeting and melting into one another, this becoming one instead of two, was the very thing he had long needed. The reason is that human nature was originally one and we were whole, and the desire and pursuit of the whole is called love. There was a time, I say, when we were one; but now, because of our wickedness, the god has split us apart, as the Spartans split up the Arcadians into separate villages.

And if we do not obey the gods, there is a danger that we shall be split in two again, and go about like the figures carved in low relief on monuments, shown in profile with only half a nose — like the halves of a broken token. That is why we should urge everyone to be pious toward the gods, so that we may avoid evil and obtain the good, of which Love is our lord and provider. Let no one oppose him; whoever opposes him is an enemy of the gods. For if we become friends of the god and are at peace with him, we shall find our own true loves, which few people these days do. I am serious; so I must ask Eryximachus not to make fun of me or suppose that I am hinting at Pausanias and Agathon — though I suspect that both of them are manly by nature and belong to the class I have been describing. But what I say applies to everyone, men and women everywhere. I believe that our race would be happy if love were perfectly fulfilled for us, and each of us found his own original true love and returned to his original nature. And if that would be best of all, then the best thing possible in our present circumstances must be to come as close to it as we can: to find a love whose nature suits our own.

So if we are to praise the one who gives us this benefit, we must praise the god Love, our greatest benefactor. In this life he leads us back to our own nature, and he gives us great hopes for the future: he promises that if we are pious, he will restore us to our original state, heal us, and make us happy and blessed. That, Eryximachus, is my speech about love. It is different from yours, but I must beg you not to make it a target for your jokes, so that we can hear each of the others — or rather both of them, since only Agathon and Socrates are left.

'I won't attack it,' said Eryximachus, 'for I thought your speech delightful. And if I didn't know that Agathon and Socrates are masters in matters of love, I would be really afraid that they would have nothing left to say, after so much has been said already. Even so, I have hopes.'
Socrates said: 'You played your own part well, Eryximachus. But if you were where I am now — or rather where I shall be once Agathon has spoken — you would be in serious difficulty.'
'You're trying to cast a spell on me, Socrates,' said Agathon, 'so that I'll be flustered by the thought that the audience expects me to speak well.'

'I would have a short memory, Agathon,' Socrates replied, 'if I thought a small party of friends could rattle your nerves — I, who saw your courage and confidence when you went up on the stage with your actors, just before your plays were performed, and faced that vast theater without the slightest sign of fear.'
'Surely, Socrates,' said Agathon, 'you don't think my head is so full of the theater that I don't know that, to a man of sense, a few good judges are more alarming than a crowd of fools?'

'No,' Socrates replied, 'it would be very wrong of me, Agathon, to accuse you of that or any other lack of sophistication. I am quite sure that if you met people you considered wise, you would care much more about their opinion than about the crowd's. But we can hardly count as the wise few, since we were there in the theater, part of the foolish crowd. Still, I know that if you found yourself in front of some truly wise man, rather than one of us, you would be ashamed to do anything disgraceful in front of him — wouldn't you?'
'Yes,' said Agathon.
'But in front of the crowd,' said Socrates, 'you would not be ashamed, if you thought you were doing something disgraceful in front of them?'

At this point Phaedrus interrupted them: 'My dear Agathon, don't answer him. If he can only find someone to talk with — especially someone good-looking — he'll no longer care about finishing what we set out to do. I love to hear him talk; but just now I must not forget the speech in praise of Love that I am owed by him and by every one of you. When the two of you have paid the god his tribute, then you can talk.'

'You're right, Phaedrus,' said Agathon. 'Nothing stops me from giving my speech; I'll have plenty of other chances to talk with Socrates. First I will say how I ought to speak, and then I will speak.'

chapters.title: Agathon's Speech
paragraphs: The speakers before me, instead of praising the god Love or explaining his nature, seem to have congratulated mankind on the good things he gives them. I would rather praise the god himself first, and then speak of his gifts; that is always the right way to praise anything. May I say, then, without irreverence or offense, that of all the blessed gods he is the most blessed, because he is the most beautiful and the best? He is the most beautiful: first, because he is the youngest. He proves his youth himself, by running away from Old Age — who is swift enough, swifter indeed than most of us would like. Love hates Old Age and will not come near him; but youth and love live and move together — like to like, as the proverb says. Phaedrus said many things about Love that I agree with, but I cannot agree that he is older than Iapetus and Kronos. No: I say that he is the youngest of the gods, and forever young. Those ancient doings among the gods that Hesiod and Parmenides tell of, if the stories are true, were the work of Necessity, not of Love. If Love had been there in those days, there would have been no chaining or mutilation of the gods, and no other violence, but peace and sweetness, as there has been in heaven ever since Love began to rule. Love is young, and he is also tender. It would take a poet like Homer to describe his tenderness — Homer, who says of Ate, the goddess of folly and ruin, that she is a goddess and tender:
'Her feet are tender, for she sets her steps not on the ground but on the heads of men:'

and that is an excellent proof of her tenderness: she walks not on what is hard but on what is soft. Let us offer the same kind of proof that Love is tender. He walks not on the earth, nor even on people's skulls, which are not so very soft, but in the hearts and souls of gods and men, which are the softest things there are. That is where he walks and lives and makes his home. Not in every soul without exception: where he finds hardness he leaves, and where he finds softness he stays. And since he always nestles, feet and all, and in every way, in the softest of soft places, how can he be anything but the softest of all things? So he is the most tender as well as the youngest; and his form is also supple. If he were rigid and unbending, he could not wrap himself around everything, or slip into and out of every human soul unnoticed. A proof of his suppleness and his well-proportioned form is his grace, which everyone agrees belongs to Love above all; gracelessness and love are always at war with each other. The beauty of his complexion is shown by his living among flowers; for he will not settle on anything, body or soul or anything else, that has no bloom or whose bloom is fading; but wherever there are flowers and scents, there he settles and stays. That is enough about the beauty of the god, though a great deal more remains to be said.

Now I must speak of his virtue. His greatest glory is that he never wrongs any god or any man, and is never wronged by any. If anything happens to him, it is not by force, for force does not come near him; and when he acts, he does not act by force. For everyone serves Love willingly in everything, and where both sides agree willingly there is justice, as the laws — the lords of the city — declare. And he is not only just but supremely self-controlled. Self-control, everyone agrees, is the power that rules pleasures and desires, and no pleasure is ever stronger than Love. He is their master and they are his servants; and if he masters them, he must be self-controlled indeed. As for courage, not even the God of War is a match for him. The God of War is the captive and Love the lord — for love, the love of Aphrodite, masters him, as the story goes — and the master is stronger than the servant. And if he masters the bravest of all the others, he must himself be the bravest. I have spoken of his courage, his justice and his self-control; I have still to speak of his wisdom, and I must do my best, as far as I am able. First of all — and here, like Eryximachus, I am honoring my own art — he is a poet, and he makes poets of others, which he could not do if he were not a poet himself.

At his touch everyone becomes a poet, 'even one who had no music in him before.' This, too, proves that Love is a good poet, skilled in every kind of creative art; for no one can give another what he does not have himself, or teach what he does not know. And who will deny that the making of all living creatures is his work? Are they not all products of his wisdom, born and begotten through him? As for the craftsmen, do we not know that only those whom love inspires win the light of fame, while anyone Love has not touched walks in darkness? Apollo discovered the arts of medicine, archery and divination under the guidance of love and desire, so he too is a pupil of Love. The music of the Muses, the metalwork of Hephaestus, the weaving of Athene, and Zeus's rule over gods and men are all likewise due to Love, who invented them. That is how Love brought order to the affairs of the gods — love of beauty, obviously, since Love has nothing to do with ugliness. In the old days, as I said at the start, terrible things were done among the gods, because Necessity ruled them; but ever since Love was born, every good thing in heaven and on earth has come from the Love of the beautiful. So, Phaedrus, I say that Love is himself the most beautiful and the best, and the cause of what is most beautiful and best in everything else. And a line of verse comes into my mind, which says that he is the god who
'Gives peace on earth and calms the stormy deep, who stills the winds and bids the sufferer sleep.'

It is he who empties men of unfriendliness and fills them with friendliness; who brings them together at banquets like this one, and is our lord at sacrifices, feasts and dances; who sends courtesy and sends discourtesy away; who always gives kindness and never gives unkindness. He is the friend of the good, the wonder of the wise, the marvel of the gods; longed for by those who have no share in him, and treasured by those who have the larger share. He is the parent of delicacy, luxury, desire, fondness, softness and grace; caring for the good, careless of the bad. In every word, work, wish and fear, he is our savior, pilot, comrade and helper; the glory of gods and men, leader best and brightest. Let every man follow in his footsteps, singing sweetly in his honor and joining in that sweet song with which love charms the souls of gods and men. That, Phaedrus, is my speech, half playful, yet with a certain measure of seriousness; I dedicate it to the god as well as I am able.

When Agathon had finished, Aristodemus said, everyone cheered: they thought the young man had spoken in a way worthy of himself and of the god. Socrates looked at Eryximachus and said: 'Tell me, son of Acumenus, wasn't I right to be afraid? Didn't I prophesy truly when I said that Agathon would give a wonderful speech, and that I would be left at a loss?'
'The part of your prophecy about Agathon seems true to me,' replied Eryximachus, 'but not the other part — that you will be at a loss.'

'But my dear friend,' said Socrates, 'how could I, or anyone else, not be at a loss, having to speak after hearing such a rich and varied speech? I was especially struck by the beauty of the closing words — who could listen to them without amazement? When I thought how far my own powers fall short, I was ready to run away in shame, if there had been any way to escape. For the speech reminded me of Gorgias, the great master of rhetoric; and at its end I imagined Agathon brandishing at me the head of Gorgias — a Gorgon's head, as in Homer — to turn me and my speech to stone and strike me dumb. Then I saw how foolish I had been to agree to take my turn with you in praising love, and to say that I was an expert in the subject, when I really had no idea how anything ought to be praised. In my simplicity I thought that the things said in praise should be true; and that, with this taken for granted, the speaker should choose the best of the true things and present them in the best way. And I was quite proud, thinking that I knew what true praise is and would speak well. But now I see that the idea was to attribute to Love every kind of greatness and glory, whether it really belonged to him or not, without regard for truth or falsehood — that did not matter. It seems the original proposal was not that each of you should really praise Love, but only that you should appear to praise him.

'And so you heap on Love every kind of praise that can be gathered from anywhere. You say that "he is all this" and "the cause of all that," so as to make him appear the most beautiful and the best of all — to those who don't know him, that is, since you can't deceive those who do. And a fine and solemn hymn of praise you have recited. But I misunderstood what kind of praise was meant when I agreed to take my turn, so I must ask to be released from a promise I made in ignorance — a promise, as Euripides would say, of the lips and not of the mind. So farewell to that kind of song: I do not praise that way — no, I cannot. But if you would like to hear the truth about love, I am ready to speak in my own way, though I will not make myself ridiculous by competing with your speeches. So tell me, Phaedrus, whether you want to hear the truth about love, told in whatever words and whatever order happen to come into my mind. Would that suit you?'

Aristodemus said that Phaedrus and the others told Socrates to speak in whatever way he thought best. 'Then,' Socrates went on, 'with your permission, let me first ask Agathon a few more questions, so that I can base my speech on the points he agrees to.'
'I grant the permission,' said Phaedrus. 'Put your questions.' Socrates then proceeded as follows:

chapters.title: Socrates & Diotima
paragraphs: In the magnificent speech you just gave, dear Agathon, I think you were right to begin by describing Love's nature before discussing his works — that's an approach I very much approve of. And since you've spoken so eloquently about his nature, may I ask you one more thing: is love the love of something, or of nothing? Let me explain what I mean. I do not want you to say that love is the love of a father or the love of a mother — that is, whose child Love is; that would be ridiculous. I want you to answer as you would if I asked about a father: is a father the father of something? You would have no difficulty in replying that he is the father of a son or a daughter; and the answer would be right.
'Very true,' said Agathon.
'And you would say the same of a mother?'
He assented.
'Let me ask one more question, to make my meaning clear: isn't a brother, just by being a brother, the brother of something?'
'Certainly,' he replied.
'That is, of a brother or sister?'
'Yes,' he said.
'And now,' said Socrates, 'I will ask about Love: is Love of something, or of nothing?'
'Of something, surely,' he replied.
'Keep in mind what that something is, and tell me this: does Love desire the thing he is love of?'
'Yes, surely.'
'And does he possess, or does he not possess, that which he loves and desires?'
'Probably not, I should say.'

'Consider,' replied Socrates, 'whether "necessarily" is not the right word, rather than "probably." To my mind, Agathon, it is absolutely and necessarily true that whoever desires something lacks something, and whoever desires nothing lacks nothing. What do you think?'
'I agree with you,' said Agathon.
'Very good. Would someone who is big desire to be big, or someone who is strong desire to be strong?'
'That would be inconsistent with our previous admissions.'
'True. For no one can lack what he already is?'
'Very true.'

'And yet,' Socrates went on, 'suppose a man who was strong desired to be strong, or a man who was swift desired to be swift, or a man who was healthy desired to be healthy. In that case someone might think that he desires what he already has or already is. I mention this example so that we are not misled. For these people, Agathon, must be supposed to have their advantages at the present time, whether they wish to or not — and who can desire what he already has? So when someone says, "I am healthy and wish to be healthy," or "I am rich and wish to be rich, and I desire simply to have what I have," we shall reply: "My friend, you have wealth and health and strength, and what you wish is to go on having them; for at this moment, whether you wish it or not, you have them. So when you say, 'I desire what I have and nothing else,' don't you really mean that you want to have in the future what you have now?" He must agree with us — mustn't he?'
'He must,' replied Agathon.

'Then,' said Socrates, 'he desires that what he has now should be kept for him in the future — which is the same as saying that he desires something that is not yet his, something he does not yet have.'
'Very true,' he said.

'Then he, and everyone else who desires, desires what he does not already have — what lies in the future and not the present, what he does not have and is not himself, what he lacks — and these are the kinds of things that love and desire seek?'
'Very true,' he said.
'Now then,' said Socrates, 'let us sum up the argument. First, isn't love the love of something, and of something that a man lacks?'
'Yes,' he replied.

'Remember also what you said in your speech — or, if you don't remember, I will remind you. You said that love of the beautiful brought order to the affairs of the gods, since there is no love of ugly things. Didn't you say something like that?'
'Yes,' said Agathon.
'Yes, my friend,' said Socrates, 'and you were right to say it. And if this is true, Love is love of beauty and not of ugliness?'
He assented.
'And we have already agreed that Love is love of something a man lacks and does not have?'
'True,' he said.
'Then Love lacks beauty, and does not have it?'
'Certainly,' he replied.
'And would you call something beautiful that lacks beauty and does not have it?'
'Certainly not.'
'Then would you still say that love is beautiful?'
Agathon replied: 'I fear that I did not understand what I was saying.'
'You made a very good speech, Agathon,' replied Socrates. 'But there is one more small question I would like to ask: isn't what is good also beautiful?'
'Yes.'
'Then if love lacks what is beautiful, love lacks what is good as well?'
'I cannot refute you, Socrates,' said Agathon. 'Let us assume that what you say is true.'
'Say instead, my beloved Agathon, that it is the truth you cannot refute; for Socrates is easily refuted.'

Socrates went on: And now I will let you go, and tell you about love as I once heard it from Diotima of Mantineia — a woman wise in this and in many other things, who long ago, when the Athenians offered sacrifices before the plague came, put off the disease for ten years. She was the one who taught me about love. I will repeat to you what she said to me, starting from the points Agathon has agreed to, which are nearly, if not exactly, the same as the ones I agreed to when the wise woman questioned me. I think this will be the easiest way, and I will play both parts myself, as well as I can. As you suggested, Agathon, I must first describe who Love is and what his nature is, and then his works. At first I said to her almost exactly what Agathon said to me: that Love was a great god, and beautiful as well. And she proved to me, just as I proved to him, that by my own reasoning Love was neither beautiful nor good. 'What do you mean, Diotima?' I said. 'Is love, then, bad and ugly?' 'Hush!' she said. 'Must whatever is not beautiful be ugly?' 'Of course,' I said. 'And must whatever is not wise be ignorant?' she asked. 'Don't you see that there is something in between wisdom and ignorance?' 'And what is that?' I asked.

'Correct opinion,' she replied. 'As you know, it cannot give reasons for itself, and so it is not knowledge — for how can knowledge be without reasons? Nor is it ignorance — for ignorance could never hit on the truth. Clearly, then, it is something in between ignorance and wisdom.' 'Quite true,' I replied. 'Then don't insist,' she said, 'that what is not beautiful must be ugly, or that what is not good must be bad. And don't conclude that because love is not beautiful and good, he must be ugly and bad; he is something in between.' 'Well,' I said, 'surely everyone agrees that Love is a great god.' 'Everyone who knows,' she asked, 'or everyone who doesn't know?' 'Everyone.' She smiled. 'And how, Socrates, can Love be agreed to be a great god by people who say that he is not a god at all?' 'And who are they?' I asked. 'You are one of them,' she said, 'and I am another.' 'How can that be?' I said. 'It is easy to see,' she replied. 'You would agree that the gods are happy and beautiful — of course you would. Would you dare to say that any god is not?' 'Certainly not,' I said. 'And by the happy,' she asked, 'you mean those who possess good or beautiful things?' 'Yes.' 'And you have agreed that Love, because he lacks good and beautiful things, desires the very things he lacks?' 'Yes, I have.' 'But how can anyone be a god who has no share in what is good or beautiful?' 'He can't.' 'Then you see that you, too, deny that Love is a god.'

'Then what is Love?' I asked. 'Is he mortal?' 'No,' she said. 'What, then?' I asked. 'As in the other cases, he is neither mortal nor immortal, but something in between.' 'What is he, then, Diotima?' 'A great spirit — a daimon — and, like every spirit, he is in between the divine and the mortal.' 'And what is his power?' I asked. 'He interprets between gods and men,' she replied. 'He carries across to the gods the prayers and sacrifices of men, and brings back to men the commands of the gods and their replies. He is the go-between who spans the gulf that divides them, and so in him everything is bound together. Through him pass all the arts of prophets and priests — their sacrifices, mysteries and spells, and all prophecy and magic. For the gods do not mix with human beings; all the dealings and conversation of gods with men, whether waking or asleep, are carried on through Love. The wisdom that understands this is spiritual; every other kind of wisdom, such as skill in the arts or in handicrafts, is lowly and base. These spirits, or in-between powers, are many and of many kinds, and one of them is Love.' 'And who were his father and his mother?' I asked. 'That is a long story,' she said, 'but I will tell you. On Aphrodite's birthday the gods held a feast, and one of the guests was the god Poros, or Plenty, the son of Metis, or Prudence. When the feast was over, Penia, or Poverty, came begging at the door, as beggars do at such times.

'Now Plenty, who was drunk on nectar — there was no wine in those days — went into the garden of Zeus and fell into a heavy sleep. And Poverty, thinking of how little she had, plotted to have a child by him; so she lay down beside him and conceived Love. That is why Love is Aphrodite's follower and attendant: partly because he is by nature a lover of beauty and Aphrodite herself is beautiful, and partly because he was born on her birthday. And his fortunes match his parentage. First, he is always poor, and far from being the tender and beautiful creature most people imagine; he is rough and dirty, with no shoes and no house to live in. He lies on the bare ground under the open sky, sleeping in the streets or in doorways; like his mother, he is always in need. But like his father, whom he also partly resembles, he is always scheming to win the beautiful and the good. He is bold, enterprising and strong, a mighty hunter, always weaving some plot or other; eager for wisdom and full of resources; a lover of wisdom all his life, and a formidable enchanter, sorcerer and sophist. By nature he is neither mortal nor immortal: at one moment, when he has plenty, he is alive and flourishing; at another he is dead; and then, thanks to his father's nature, he comes back to life again.

'But what flows in is always flowing out again, so he is never without resources and never rich. And he is also in between ignorance and knowledge. This is how it is: no god is a philosopher or seeks wisdom, for the gods are wise already; nor does anyone else who is wise seek wisdom. But the ignorant do not seek wisdom either. For this is what is so bad about ignorance: someone who is neither good nor wise is nevertheless satisfied with himself — he does not desire what he does not feel he lacks.' 'Then who are the lovers of wisdom, Diotima,' I asked, 'if they are neither the wise nor the foolish?' 'Even a child could tell you,' she replied. 'They are those in between the two, and Love is one of them. For wisdom is a most beautiful thing, and Love is love of the beautiful; so Love must be a philosopher, a lover of wisdom, and as a lover of wisdom he is in between the wise and the ignorant. His birth is the cause of this too: his father is wealthy and wise, and his mother poor and foolish. That, my dear Socrates, is the nature of the spirit Love. Your mistaken idea of him was quite natural. Judging from what you say, I imagine it came from confusing love with the beloved, which made you think that love was altogether beautiful. For it is the beloved that is truly beautiful, delicate, perfect and blessed; but what loves is of a different nature, the one I have described.'

I said, 'Well said, my foreign friend. But if Love is as you say, what use is he to human beings?' 'That, Socrates,' she replied, 'is what I will try to explain next. I have told you about his nature and his birth, and you agree that love is love of the beautiful. But suppose someone asks us, "Of the beautiful — in what sense, Socrates and Diotima?" Or let me put the question more clearly: when someone loves the beautiful, what does he desire?' I answered, 'That the beautiful may be his.' 'But that answer,' she said, 'raises a further question: what does he gain by possessing beauty?' 'I have no answer ready for that question,' I replied. 'Then,' she said, 'let me put the word "good" in place of "beautiful" and ask the question again: if someone who loves, loves the good, what is it that he loves?' 'To possess the good,' I said. 'And what does someone gain by possessing the good?' she asked. 'Happiness,' I replied. 'That question is easier to answer.' 'Yes,' she said, 'for the happy are happy because they have acquired good things. And there is no need to ask further why someone desires happiness; that answer is final.' 'You are right,' I said.

'And is this wish, this desire, shared by everyone?' she asked. 'Do all people always desire their own good, or only some? What do you say?' 'All people,' I replied. 'The desire is common to all.' 'Then why is it, Socrates,' she asked, 'that we do not say that everyone loves, but only some people — if, as you say, everyone always loves the same things?' 'I wonder about that myself,' I said. 'There is nothing to wonder at,' she replied. 'The reason is that we separate off one part of love and give it the name of the whole, while the other parts have other names.' 'Give me an example,' I said. She answered: 'Take poetry. As you know, it covers many different things. All creation — every passage from not being into being — is "poetry," that is, making; the processes of all the arts are creative, and all the masters of the arts are "poets," that is, makers.' 'True.' 'But you know,' she said, 'that they are not called poets; they have other names. One part of making has been separated off from the rest — the part that has to do with music and verse — and only this is called poetry, and only those who practice it are called poets.' 'True,' I said. She went on: 'And it is the same with love.

'For, speaking generally, every desire for good things and for happiness is love — the great and subtle power of love. But those who turn to him along some other path, whether money-making or physical training or philosophy, are not called lovers. The name of the whole is reserved for those whose desire takes one particular form: they alone are said to love, or are called lovers.' 'I dare say you are right,' I replied. 'Yes,' she went on, 'and you hear people say that lovers are looking for their other half. But I say that they are looking neither for their own half nor for the whole, unless the half or the whole is also something good. People will even cut off their own hands and feet and throw them away if they are bad; for people do not love what is their own, unless perhaps someone calls what belongs to him good and what belongs to another bad. For there is nothing that people love except the good. Or is there?' 'Certainly not, I would say.' 'Then,' she said, 'the simple truth is that people love the good.' 'Yes,' I said. 'And we must add that they love to possess the good?' she asked. 'Yes, we must add that.' 'And not only to possess it,' she asked, 'but to possess it forever?' 'We must add that too.' 'Then in short,' she said, 'love is the love of possessing the good forever?' 'That is very true.'

'Then if this is the nature of love,' she said, 'can you tell me more: in what way do people pursue it? What are people doing when they show all the eagerness and intensity that is called love? What is it they are trying to achieve? Answer me.' 'No, Diotima,' I replied. 'If I knew, I would not be marveling at your wisdom, or have come to you to learn about these very things.' 'Well,' she said, 'I will teach you. What they are aiming at is giving birth in beauty, whether in body or in soul.' 'I don't understand,' I said. 'Your oracle needs interpreting.' 'I will put it more clearly,' she replied. 'What I mean is that all human beings are pregnant, in body and in soul. When we reach a certain age, human nature desires to give birth; but it must give birth in beauty, and not in ugliness. The union of a man and a woman is such a giving birth, and it is a divine thing; for conception and procreation are an immortal element in the mortal creature, and they can never happen in what is out of harmony. The ugly is always out of harmony with the divine, and the beautiful in harmony with it.

'So Beauty is the Fate, or goddess of childbirth, who presides at birth. That is why, when the creature that has conceived comes near beauty, it grows gracious, relaxed and kindly, and begets and bears fruit; but at the sight of ugliness it frowns and contracts in pain, turns away and shrivels up, and, not without a pang, holds back from giving birth. And that is why, when the time for birth comes and the pregnant creature is full to bursting, there is such excitement and ecstasy about beauty: its coming eases the pains of labor. For love, Socrates, is not, as you think, love of the beautiful only.' 'What, then?' I asked. 'The love of procreation and of giving birth in beauty.' 'Yes,' I said. 'Yes, indeed,' she replied. 'But why of procreation?' I asked. 'Because for a mortal creature, procreation is a kind of eternity and immortality,' she replied. 'And if, as we have already agreed, love is love of possessing the good forever, everyone must necessarily desire immortality together with the good. So love is love of immortality.'

She taught me all this at various times when she spoke about love. And I remember her once saying to me, 'What is the cause, Socrates, of love, and of the desire that goes with it? Don't you see how all animals, birds as well as beasts, are in agony when they catch the fever of love through their desire to breed? First they long to mate with one another, and then they long to care for their young. For their young the weakest are ready to fight the strongest to the very end, and even to die for them; they will starve themselves or suffer anything else to rear them. With human beings, one might suppose that they act this way from reason; but why should animals feel such passion? Can you tell me why?' Again I said that I did not know. She said to me: 'And do you expect ever to become an expert in love, if you don't know this?' 'But Diotima, as I told you before, that is exactly why I came to you — because I know that I need a teacher. So tell me the cause of this, and of the other mysteries of love.' 'There is nothing to be surprised at,' she said, 'if you believe that love is love of immortality, as we have agreed several times. For here too, on the same principle, mortal nature seeks, as far as it can, to be everlasting and immortal. And it can achieve this only through procreation, because procreation always leaves behind something new in place of the old.

'Indeed, even in the life of one and the same individual there is succession, not complete sameness. A man is called the same person from youth to old age — through the whole short span in which each living creature is said to live and to be the same — and yet all the while he is constantly losing and renewing himself: his hair, flesh, bones, blood and whole body are always changing. And this is true not only of the body but of the soul as well. None of us keeps the same habits, character, opinions, desires, pleasures, pains or fears; they are always coming and going.
