It is true of knowledge too, and, what is even more surprising to us mortals, not only do our branches of knowledge as a whole come and go, so that we are never the same even in what we know, but each single one of them goes through the same change. For what does the word "recollection" imply, if not that knowledge departs? Knowledge is always being forgotten, and it is renewed and preserved by recollection, so that it seems to be the same, though in reality it is new. That is the law of succession by which all mortal things are preserved: not by remaining absolutely the same, but by replacement, as the old and worn-out leaves behind something new and similar in its place — unlike the divine, which is always the same and never another. In this way, Socrates, the mortal body, and every other mortal thing, shares in immortality; the immortal does so in a different way.
'So do not be surprised at the love that all people have for their offspring; that universal love and care is for the sake of immortality.'

I was amazed at what she said, and asked, 'Is this really true, wise Diotima?' And she answered with all the authority of an accomplished sophist: 'You can be sure of it, Socrates. Just think of people's ambition: you will be amazed at how senseless their behavior is, unless you consider how they are stirred by love of an immortal name. For the sake of leaving behind a name that will last forever, they are ready to run every risk — far greater risks than they would run for their children — and to spend money, endure any hardship, and even die. Do you suppose that Alcestis would have died to save Admetus, or Achilles to avenge Patroclus, or your own Athenian king Codrus to preserve the kingdom for his sons, if they had not expected that the memory of their virtue, which we still keep, would be immortal? Far from it,' she said. 'I am convinced that everyone does everything in the hope of the glorious fame of immortal virtue — and the better they are, the more they do so; for they desire what is immortal.

'Those who are pregnant only in body turn to women and have children — that is how their love works — hoping that their children will keep their memory alive and give them, in the future, the happiness and immortality they desire. But there are also souls that are pregnant — for there certainly are men who are more creative in their souls than in their bodies — and they conceive what it is fitting for the soul to conceive and to carry. And what is that? Wisdom and virtue in general. Creators of this kind are the poets, and all those craftsmen who deserve to be called inventors. But by far the greatest and most beautiful kind of wisdom is the one concerned with the good ordering of cities and households, which is called self-control and justice. And when someone has had the seed of these planted in him in his youth, and is himself inspired, then, when he comes of age, he desires to beget and give birth.

'He goes about seeking beauty so that he may beget offspring, for he will never beget in ugliness; and so he naturally embraces beautiful bodies rather than ugly ones. And above all, if he finds a soul that is beautiful, noble and well nurtured, he embraces the two combined in one person. To such a person he is full of things to say about virtue, and about the nature and pursuits of a good man; and he tries to educate him. At the touch of someone beautiful, whom he keeps in mind even when they are apart, he brings forth what he has long carried within him, and together with his companion he raises what is born. Such people are wedded by a far nearer tie, and share a closer friendship, than those who have mortal children, because the children they share are more beautiful and more immortal. Who, thinking of Homer and Hesiod and the other great poets, would not rather have children like theirs than ordinary human ones? Who would not want to rival them in producing children like theirs, which have preserved their memory and given them everlasting glory? Or who would not want children like those Lycurgus left behind him — his laws — to be the saviors not only of Sparta but, one might say, of Greece?

'And there is Solon, the revered father of Athenian laws; and there are many others in many other places, among Greeks and barbarians alike, who have given the world many noble works and fathered virtue of every kind. Many temples have been raised in their honor because of such children as these; none has ever been raised in anyone's honor because of his mortal children.

'These are the lesser mysteries of love, and even you, Socrates, may be initiated into them. But I do not know whether you could attain the greater and more hidden mysteries, which are the crown of these, and to which these will lead if you pursue them in the right spirit. Still, I will do my very best to explain them to you; try to follow if you can. Whoever means to go about this rightly must begin in his youth by turning to beautiful bodies. First, if his guide leads him rightly, he must love one such body only, and out of that love give birth to beautiful thoughts. Soon he will see for himself that the beauty of one body is akin to the beauty of another; and then, if it is bodily beauty in general that he is pursuing, how foolish he would be not to recognize that the beauty in every body is one and the same! Once he sees this, he will relax his intense love for the one, looking down on it as a small thing, and will become a lover of all beautiful bodies. At the next stage, he will come to value the beauty of the soul above the beauty of the body.

'So if he finds someone with a virtuous soul, even if that person has little bodily beauty, he will be content to love and care for him, and to seek out and give birth to the kind of thoughts that make the young better, until he is compelled in turn to contemplate the beauty of practices and laws, and to see that all this beauty is of one family, and that bodily beauty is a trifling thing. After practices and laws, he will go on to the branches of knowledge, so that he may see their beauty too. He will not be like a servant in love with the beauty of one youth or one man or one practice — himself a slave, petty and narrow-minded. Instead, turning toward the vast sea of beauty and contemplating it, he will give birth to many beautiful and noble thoughts and ideas in a boundless love of wisdom, until, grown and strengthened on that shore, he at last catches sight of a single kind of knowledge: the knowledge of beauty everywhere. I will go on to describe it now; please give me your very closest attention.

'Whoever has been taught this far in the things of love, and has learned to see beautiful things in their proper order, one after another, will suddenly, as he nears the end, catch sight of a nature of wonderful beauty — and this, Socrates, is what all our earlier labors were for. First, it is everlasting: it does not grow and decay, or increase and diminish. Second, it is not beautiful from one point of view and ugly from another; not beautiful at one time and ugly at another, or beautiful in one relation and ugly in another, or beautiful in one place and ugly in another, as if it were beautiful to some and ugly to others. Nor is it in the likeness of a face or hands or any other part of the body, or in any form of speech or knowledge; nor does it exist in any other being — in an animal, for example, or in heaven, or on earth, or anywhere else. It is beauty itself: absolute, separate, simple and everlasting. Without being diminished or increased, or changed in any way, it is imparted to the beauties of all other things, which are always growing and perishing. Whoever rises from these things under the influence of true love, and begins to see that beauty, is not far from the end.

'And the true order of approaching the things of love, or of being led to them by another, is to begin from the beautiful things of this world and mount upward for the sake of that other beauty, using them only as steps — from one beautiful body to two, and from two to all beautiful bodies; from beautiful bodies to beautiful practices, and from beautiful practices to beautiful branches of knowledge; until from these he arrives at the knowledge of absolute beauty, and knows at last what the essence of beauty is. This, my dear Socrates,' said the woman from Mantineia, 'is the life above all others that a human being should live: in the contemplation of absolute beauty. If you ever saw it, you would see that it is not to be measured against gold, or fine clothes, or beautiful boys and youths — the ones whose presence now so entrances you that you, and many others, would be content, if it were possible, to go without food and drink, only to look at them and be with them. But what if someone had eyes to see true beauty — divine beauty, I mean, pure, clear and unmixed, not tainted by mortality or by all the colors and vanities of human life — and could look at the true beauty, simple and divine, and be in its company?

'Remember that only in that communion, seeing beauty with the eye of the mind, will he be able to bring forth not images of beauty but realities, because what he has hold of is not an image but reality. And by bringing forth true virtue and nourishing it, he will be able to become a friend of the gods, and immortal, if any mortal can be. Would that be a life to despise?'

That, Phaedrus — and I say it not only to you but to all of you — is what Diotima told me, and I am convinced that it is true. And because I am convinced, I try to convince others as well that, for reaching this goal, human nature could not easily find a better helper than love. That is why I say that everyone ought to honor him, as I myself honor him, and follow his ways, and urge others to do the same; and now and always I praise the power and spirit of love as far as I am able.
You may call what I have said, Phaedrus, an encomium — a speech in praise of love — or anything else you like.

chapters.title: Alcibiades
paragraphs: When Socrates had finished speaking, everyone applauded, and Aristophanes was starting to answer the allusion Socrates had made to Aristophanes's own speech, when suddenly there was a loud knocking at the front door, as if from a band of revelers, and the sound of a flute-girl could be heard. Agathon told the attendants to go and see who was there. 'If they are friends of ours,' he said, 'invite them in; if not, say that the drinking is over.' A moment later they heard the voice of Alcibiades in the courtyard. He was very drunk, and kept roaring and shouting, 'Where's Agathon? Take me to Agathon!' At last, held up by the flute-girl and some of his attendants, he found his way to them. He stood in the doorway, crowned with a thick wreath of ivy and violets, with a mass of ribbons streaming from his head. 'Greetings, friends,' he said. 'Will you let a very drunk man join your party? Or shall I just crown Agathon — which is what I came for — and go away? I couldn't come yesterday, so I'm here today, with these ribbons on my head, so that I can take them off my own head and crown the head of the most beautiful and wisest of men — if I may call him that. Are you going to laugh at me because I'm drunk? Laugh if you like; I know very well that I'm telling the truth. But first tell me: if I come in, do we have an agreement, on the terms I mentioned?
'Will you drink with me or not?'

Everyone shouted to him to come in and take a place among them, and Agathon invited him in particular. So his companions led him in. As he was being led in, meaning to crown Agathon, he took the ribbons off his own head and held them up in front of his eyes, so that he did not see Socrates, who made room for him. So Alcibiades took the empty place between Agathon and Socrates, and as he did so he embraced Agathon and crowned him. 'Take off his sandals,' said Agathon, 'and let him make a third on our couch.'

'By all means,' said Alcibiades. 'But who is our third companion here?' He turned around, and when he saw Socrates he leaped up. 'By Heracles,' he said, 'what's this? Socrates, lying in wait for me again, as always, and turning up, as you always do, where I least expect you! What have you got to say for yourself? And why are you lying here? I see you've contrived to find a place not next to some joker or lover of jokes, like Aristophanes, but next to the most beautiful person in the room!'

Socrates turned to Agathon and said: 'Agathon, I must ask you to protect me, because this man's passion has become a serious problem for me. Ever since I fell for him, I haven't been allowed to talk to anyone else who is beautiful, or even to look at them. If I do, he goes wild with envy and jealousy; he shouts abuse at me and can hardly keep his hands off me. Even now he may do me some harm. Please see to it: either make peace between us, or, if he turns violent, protect me, because I am physically afraid of his mad and passionate attacks.'

'There can never be peace between you and me,' said Alcibiades. 'But I'll put off your punishment for now. Agathon, give me back some of those ribbons, so that I can crown this man's marvelous head too — the head of this tyrant over us all. I don't want him to complain that I crowned you and left him out, when in argument he conquers the whole human race — and not just once, as you did the day before yesterday, but always.' With that he took some of the ribbons, crowned Socrates, and lay back down.

Then he said: 'Well, my friends, you look sober to me, and that is not to be tolerated. You must drink — that was the agreement on which I was let in — and I appoint myself master of the drinking until you are all properly drunk. Agathon, let's have a large cup — or no,' he said, turning to the attendant, 'bring me that wine-cooler.' The wine-cooler that had caught his eye held more than two quarts. He had it filled, drank it off, and then told the attendant to fill it again for Socrates. 'Notice, my friends,' said Alcibiades, 'that this clever trick of mine won't work on Socrates: he can drink any amount of wine and never be any nearer to being drunk.' Socrates drank the cup the attendant filled for him.
Eryximachus said: 'What is this, Alcibiades? Are we to have neither conversation nor singing over our cups, but simply to drink as if we were thirsty?'
Alcibiades replied: 'Greetings, excellent son of a most wise and excellent father!'
'The same to you,' said Eryximachus; 'but what shall we do?'
'That I leave to you,' said Alcibiades. 'In Homer's words,
'"The wise physician skilled our wounds to heal"
'shall prescribe, and we will obey. What do you want?'

'Well,' said Eryximachus, 'before you arrived we had agreed that each of us in turn, going around from left to right, should make a speech in praise of love, the best he could. All the rest of us have spoken. You haven't spoken, though you have certainly done your drinking, so it's only fair that you should speak; and then you can give Socrates any task you like, and he can do the same to the man on his right, and so on.'

'That's a good idea, Eryximachus,' said Alcibiades. 'But it's hardly fair to set a drunk man's speech against the speeches of sober men. And tell me, my dear friend, do you really believe what Socrates said just now? I assure you the truth is the exact opposite: if I praise anyone but him while he is here, god or man, he can hardly keep his hands off me.'
'For shame,' said Socrates.
'Hold your tongue,' said Alcibiades. 'By Poseidon, there is no one else I will praise while you are here.'
'Well then,' said Eryximachus, 'if you like, praise Socrates.'
'What do you think, Eryximachus?' said Alcibiades. 'Shall I attack him and inflict the punishment before you all?'
'What are you up to?' said Socrates. 'Are you going to make fun of me? Is that what your praise is for?'
'I am going to speak the truth, if you will permit me.'
'I not only permit, but exhort you to speak the truth.'

'Then I'll begin at once,' said Alcibiades. 'And if I say anything untrue, interrupt me if you like and say, "That's a lie!" — though I mean to tell the truth. But don't be surprised if things come out in a jumble, as they come into my head; it's not easy for a man in my condition to list all your oddities fluently and in order.'

And now, my friends, I shall praise Socrates by means of an image. He will think it a caricature, but I'm using it for the sake of the truth, not to make fun of him. I say that he is exactly like the busts of Silenus you see in the sculptors' shops, with pipes and flutes in their mouths: they are made to open down the middle, and inside they have images of gods. And I say that he is also like Marsyas the satyr. You yourself will not deny, Socrates, that your face is like a satyr's. And you are like them in other ways too. For one thing, you are insolent — I can bring witnesses to prove it if you won't admit it. And aren't you a flute-player? You certainly are — and a far more wonderful one than Marsyas. He charmed people's souls with instruments, by the power of his breath, and those who play his music still do: for the melodies of Olympus, Marsyas's pupil, come from Marsyas, who taught them to him. Whether a great master plays them or a second-rate flute-girl, these melodies have a power no others have: they alone take possession of people's souls and reveal which of them are in need of the gods and their mysteries, because the melodies are divine. But you have the same effect with words alone, without any flute; that is the difference between you and him.

When we hear any other speaker, even a very good one, he has no effect on us at all, or hardly any; but you, and even mere fragments of your words at second hand, however badly repeated, amaze and take possession of the souls of every man, woman and child who hears them. If I weren't afraid that you would think me completely drunk, I would swear on oath, as well as tell you, what an effect these words have always had on me, and still have. When I hear them, my heart pounds harder than a Corybant's in the frenzy of the dance, and tears pour from my eyes; and I see that many others are affected the same way. I have heard Pericles and other great orators, and I thought they spoke well, but I never felt anything like this: my soul was not stirred by them, nor was I angry at the thought of my own slavish state. But this Marsyas here has often brought me to the point where I felt I could hardly bear to go on living as I do — you will admit that, Socrates. And I know that if I did not stop my ears against him and run away as if from the Sirens' song, the same thing would happen to me as to others: he would hold me spellbound, and I would grow old sitting at his feet. For he makes me admit that I ought not to live as I do, neglecting what my own soul lacks while I busy myself with the affairs of Athens. So I stop my ears and tear myself away from him.

He is the only person who has ever made me feel ashamed — you might not think I had it in me — and no one else does. For I know that I cannot argue with him or deny that I ought to do what he tells me; but when I leave him, my love of popularity gets the better of me. So I run away from him, and when I see him I am ashamed of what I have admitted to him. Many times I have wished that he were dead; and yet I know that if he died I would be far more sorry than glad. So I am at my wit's end.

That is what I and many others have suffered from this satyr's flute-playing. But listen once more while I show you how exactly the image fits him, and how marvelous his power is. For let me tell you: none of you knows him; but I will reveal him to you — having begun, I must go on. You see how fond he is of beautiful people? He is always with them and always being smitten by them; and then again he knows nothing and is ignorant of everything — that is the appearance he puts on. Isn't that just like a Silenus? Of course it is: that is his outer mask, the carved head of the Silenus. But, my fellow drinkers, when he is opened up, what self-control there is inside! Believe me, beauty and wealth and honor, which most people admire, mean nothing to him; he utterly despises them. He does not care in the least about the people who have them — human beings are nothing to him — and he spends his whole life mocking and jeering at them. But when I opened him up and looked inside at his serious purpose, I saw in him images so divine and golden, and of such enchanting beauty, that I was ready to do at once whatever Socrates told me. Others may not have noticed them, but I saw them. Now I imagined that he was seriously in love with my good looks, and I thought this gave me a wonderful opportunity to hear him tell what he knew; for I had an amazingly high opinion of the attractions of my youth.

With this plan in mind, the next time I went to him I sent away the attendant who usually came with me — I will tell you the whole truth, so listen; and if I say anything false, Socrates, expose it. So he and I were alone together, and I thought that now that there was nobody with us, he would talk to me the way lovers talk to their beloveds when they are alone, and I was delighted. Nothing of the sort. He talked as he always did, spent the day with me, and then went away. Next I asked him to come and wrestle with me at the wrestling school, and he wrestled and grappled with me several times, when no one else was there; I thought I might get somewhere that way. Not at all; I got nowhere with him. Finally, since everything had failed so far, I decided that I must use stronger measures and attack him boldly, and, having begun, not give up until I found out how things stood between us. So I invited him to dinner, just as if he were a beautiful youth and I a lover with designs on him. He was slow to accept, but after a while he did come. The first time, he wanted to leave as soon as dinner was over, and I was too embarrassed to keep him. The second time, still following my plan, I kept him talking after dinner far into the night, and when he wanted to go, I pretended that it was late and that he had much better stay.

So he lay down on the couch next to mine, the same one he had lain on at dinner, and there was no one sleeping in the room but the two of us. Up to this point I could tell the story to anyone without shame. But what comes next I could hardly tell you if I were sober. Still, as the saying goes, 'wine and boys tell the truth' — and wine does, with boys or without them; and so I must speak. Besides, having set out to praise Socrates, I would be wrong to hide his lofty actions. And there is this too: I am like someone bitten by a snake. People say that a man who has been bitten will talk about it only to others who have been bitten, because they alone are likely to understand him and will not judge him harshly for whatever his pain drove him to say and do. Well, I have been bitten by something worse than a viper, in my soul, or my heart, or some other part of me — by the worst pain there is, which strikes a young and gifted soul more fiercely than any snake: the pain of philosophy, which will make a man say or do anything. And all of you I see around me — Phaedrus and Agathon and Eryximachus and Pausanias and Aristodemus and Aristophanes, and I need not mention Socrates himself — have shared the same madness and passion in your longing for wisdom. So listen, and forgive what I did then and what I am saying now. But the attendants, and anyone else uninitiated and uncouth, must shut the doors of their ears.

When the lamp had been put out and the servants had gone, I decided I must speak plainly to him and stop hinting. So I gave him a shake and said, 'Socrates, are you asleep?' 'No,' he said. 'Do you know what I have been thinking?' I asked. 'What have you been thinking?' he said. 'I think,' I said, 'that of all the lovers I have ever had, you are the only one worthy of me, and you seem too modest to speak up. Now, this is how I feel: I would be a fool to refuse you this or any other favor. So I have come to lay at your feet everything I have and everything my friends have, in the hope that you will help me on the path to virtue, which I desire above all things; and I believe that no one can help me better than you. And I would certainly be more ashamed of what wise men would say if I refused a favor to a man like you, than of what the crowd — who are mostly fools — would say if I granted it.' When he heard this, he answered in the ironic way that is so typical of him: 'My dear Alcibiades, you are aiming high indeed, if what you say about me is true and there really is some power in me that could make you better. You must see in me some rare beauty, of a kind infinitely higher than the beauty I see in you. So if you mean to share with me and exchange beauty for beauty, you would be getting much the better of the bargain: you would be gaining true beauty in return for its mere appearance — like Diomedes in Homer, who traded bronze armor for gold.

'But look again, my dear friend, and make sure you are not mistaken about me. The mind's eye begins to see sharply when the body's eyes begin to fail, and you are a long way from that yet.' Hearing this, I said, 'I have told you my intentions, and I am quite serious. Now you consider what you think is best for you and for me.' 'That is a good answer,' he said. 'Some other time, then, we will consider and do whatever seems best about this and about other matters.' At this I imagined that he was smitten, and that my words had struck him like arrows and wounded him. So without waiting to hear more, I got up, threw my cloak over him — it was winter — and crept under his threadbare cloak; and there I lay all night with my arms around this truly extraordinary creature. You won't deny that either, Socrates. And yet, for all that, he was so far above my advances, so contemptuous and mocking and disdainful of my beauty — which I really thought had some attractions — listen, judges; for you shall be the judges of Socrates's haughty virtue — nothing more happened. When I woke up in the morning — let all the gods and goddesses be my witnesses — I got up as if I had slept beside my father or an elder brother.

What do you suppose I felt after being rejected like that, thinking of my humiliation? And yet I could not help admiring his natural self-control and restraint and courage. I had never imagined I could meet a man with such wisdom and endurance. So I could not be angry with him or give up his company, any more than I could hope to win him over. I knew very well that money could wound him even less than steel could wound Ajax; and my only chance of capturing him, by my good looks, had failed. So I was at my wit's end: no one was ever more hopelessly enslaved to another. All this happened before he and I went on the campaign to Potidaea. There we ate together in the same mess, and I had the chance to observe his extraordinary capacity for hardship. His endurance was simply marvelous when we were cut off from our supplies and had to go without food, as often happens in war: at such times he outdid not only me but everyone else; there was no one to compare with him. Yet when there was feasting, he was the only one who could really enjoy it. He did not want to drink, but when he was made to, he could outdrink us all — and, wonderful to relate, no one had ever seen Socrates drunk. His powers in that line, if I am not mistaken, will be tested before long. He was also astonishingly tough in enduring the cold.

There was a severe frost — the winters there are terrible — and everyone else either stayed indoors or, if they went out, wrapped themselves in an amazing quantity of clothes, put on shoes, and bound their feet in felt and sheepskins. But in the middle of all this, Socrates went out barefoot on the ice, in the same cloak he always wore, and marched better than the other soldiers in their shoes; and they glared at him, because they thought he was showing contempt for them.
I have told you one story, and now I must tell you another, which is worth hearing — a tale, as Homer puts it,
'Of the doings and sufferings of the enduring man'

while he was on that campaign. One morning he began thinking about a problem he could not solve. He would not give it up, but went on thinking from early dawn until noon, standing fixed to the spot, lost in thought. By noon people had noticed him, and word went around among the astonished soldiers that Socrates had been standing there thinking about something since daybreak. At last, in the evening after dinner, some Ionian soldiers, out of curiosity, brought their sleeping mats outside (this was in summer, I should explain, not winter) and slept in the open air so that they could watch him and see whether he would stand there all night. He stood there until the next morning; and when the sun came up, he said a prayer to the sun and went on his way. And if you like, I will tell you about his courage in battle — indeed, I owe it to him to tell it; for who but he saved my life? It was in the battle for which I received the prize for valor. I was wounded, and he would not leave me; he rescued both me and my weapons. He ought to have received the prize himself, and I told the generals so — Socrates will not dispute or deny this either — but the generals wanted to give it to me, partly because of my rank, and he was even more eager than they were that I, and not he, should have it.

There was another occasion on which his behavior was very remarkable: when the army was in flight after the battle of Delium. He was serving there as a heavy-armed foot soldier, and I had an even better chance to watch him than at Potidaea, because I was on horseback and so comparatively out of danger. He and Laches were retreating, since the troops were in flight; I came upon them, told them not to lose heart, and promised to stay with them. And there you could see him, Aristophanes, just as you describe him in your comedy, and just as he is in the streets of Athens, stalking like a pelican and glancing from side to side, calmly surveying friends and enemies alike, and making it very clear to anyone, even from a distance, that whoever attacked this man would be likely to meet with a stout defense. That is how he and his companion got away; for in war people never touch men like that; they pursue only those who are running away headlong. I particularly noticed how much more composed he was than Laches. There are many other marvelous things I could tell in praise of Socrates. Most of his ways could perhaps be matched in someone else; but what is truly astonishing is that he is utterly unlike any human being who exists now or has ever existed.

You might say that Brasidas and others were like Achilles, or that Nestor and Antenor were like Pericles; and the same can be done with other famous men. But you will never find anyone like this strange man, or even remotely like him, among the people who are alive now or who have ever lived — except the figures I have already suggested, Silenus and the satyrs; and they represent, in an image, not only the man himself but his words. I forgot to mention this before: his words, too, are like the busts of Silenus that open up. When you first hear them they are ridiculous; he wraps himself in language like the hide of an insolent satyr. He talks about pack-donkeys and blacksmiths and shoemakers and tanners, and he is always repeating the same things in the same words, so that anyone ignorant or inexperienced might want to laugh at him. But whoever opens the bust and sees what is inside will find that his words are the only ones that have any sense in them, and also the most divine, full of beautiful images of virtue and of the widest reach — or rather, extending to the whole duty of a good and honorable man.

That, my friends, is my praise of Socrates; and I have added my complaints about how badly he has treated me. And I am not the only one he has treated this way: he has done the same to Charmides, the son of Glaucon, and Euthydemus, the son of Diocles, and many others. He begins as their lover, and ends by making them court him instead. So I say to you, Agathon: 'Don't be deceived by him. Learn from me and take warning; don't be the fool in the proverb who learns only by experience.'

When Alcibiades had finished, there was laughter at his frankness, for he seemed to be still in love with Socrates. 'You're sober, Alcibiades,' said Socrates. 'Otherwise you would never have gone so far out of your way to hide the purpose of your satyr's praises. This whole long story is just a clever roundabout way of getting to the point, which you slipped in at the end, as if in passing: you want to stir up a quarrel between Agathon and me, and your idea is that I ought to love you and nobody else, and that you, and you alone, ought to love Agathon. But we have seen through the plot of this satyr play of yours — this Silenus drama. Agathon, don't let him set us against each other.'
'I think you're right,' said Agathon. 'I suspect that the only reason he lay down between you and me was to separate us. But he won't gain anything by it: I will come and lie down next to you.'
'Yes, yes,' said Socrates, 'by all means come and lie here, on my other side.'
'Look how this man makes a fool of me!' said Alcibiades. 'He's determined to get the better of me at every turn. Please, I beg you, let Agathon lie between us.'

'Certainly not,' said Socrates. 'You have praised me, and now it's my turn to praise the man on my right. If Agathon lies between us, it will be out of order for him to praise me again, when he ought instead to be praised by me. So I beg you to agree to this and not be jealous, because I very much want to praise this youth.'
'Hurrah!' cried Agathon. 'I'll get up at once, so that Socrates can praise me.'
'The same old story,' said Alcibiades. 'Wherever Socrates is, nobody else has a chance with beautiful people. And look how readily he has made up a plausible excuse for drawing Agathon to his side!'

Agathon was getting up to take a place on the couch beside Socrates when suddenly a crowd of revelers burst in, throwing the whole party into confusion. Someone leaving had left the front door open, and they poured in without ceremony. The noise was tremendous, all order vanished, and everyone was forced to drink enormous quantities of wine. Aristodemus said that Eryximachus, Phaedrus, and some others left at that point, while he himself fell asleep and slept for a long time — the nights were long at that season. He woke near dawn, as the cocks were crowing, and saw that most of the company were either asleep or had gone. Only Agathon, Aristophanes, and Socrates were still awake, drinking from a large bowl that they passed around from left to right. Socrates was arguing with them. Aristodemus couldn't remember most of what was said — he'd missed the beginning and was still half asleep — but the gist was that Socrates was forcing them to admit that the same person could be skilled at writing both comedy and tragedy, and that a true master of tragedy must also be a master of comedy. They were being compelled to agree, though they weren't entirely following the argument and kept nodding off. Aristophanes fell asleep first, and then, as daylight was breaking, Agathon. Socrates, having put them both to sleep, got up and left. Aristodemus followed him, as was his habit. Socrates went to the Lyceum, bathed, and spent the rest of the day as usual. In the evening, he went home to bed.
